doc_name: Dove World Outreach Center Quran-burning controversy
text: In July 2010, Terry Jones, pastor of the Dove World Outreach Center in Gainesville, Florida, announced plans to burn 200 copies of the Quran on the ninth anniversary of the September 11 attacks, which he called "International Burn a Quran Day." The announcement sparked widespread media coverage and international outrage, particularly in the Islamic world, with numerous world leaders urging Jones to cancel the event. The threat led to protests across the Middle East and Asia, resulting in at least 20 deaths. In early September 2010, Jones stated the event was canceled and pledged not to burn the Quran. However, on March 20, 2011, Jones held a "trial of the Quran" at his church in Gainesville, declaring the Quran guilty of crimes against humanity and burning it in the sanctuary. This act triggered widespread protests in Afghanistan, including a violent attack in Mazar-i-Sharif where demonstrators stormed a United Nations compound, killing at least 30 people, including seven UN staff members and more than 150 injured, with Norwegian, Swedish, Nepalese, and Romanian nationals among the victims. On April 4, 2011, two U.S. soldiers were killed by an Afghan police officer, an incident attributed to outrage over the Quran burning. American news analysts criticized Afghan President Hamid Karzai for drawing attention to the Quran burning. Terry Jones was born in October 1951 in Cape Girardeau, Missouri. He attended college for two years, worked at a hotel, and joined the now-defunct Maranatha Campus Ministries. In 1981, he founded the Christian Community of Cologne (CGK) in Cologne, Germany. In 1983, he received an honorary degree from an unaccredited theology school and began using the title "Doctor," which led to a fine from a German administrative court. By the late 2000s, the CGK had approximately 800–1000 members. According to Der Spiegel, the congregation expelled Jones in 2008 due to a "climate of fear and control," including elements of "brainwashing" and instructing congregants to beat their children with rods. He was accused of improper use of church funds and forcing congregants to labor for free. A leader of the Cologne church stated Jones did not project biblical values but made himself the center of everything, with others accusing him of being violent and fanatical. Deutsche Presse-Agentur reported church members said Jones ran the church like a cult using psychological pressure. Between 2001 and 2008, Jones served as part-time pastor of the Gainesville church, frequently traveling between Germany and the U.S., and assumed full-time duties in 2008 after leaving the German church. By September 2010, Dove World Outreach Center had about 50 members, with around 30 attending services. In 2010, Jones published a book titled Islam Is of the Devil, claiming Islam promotes violence and seeks to impose sharia in the United States. The German Evangelical Alliance denounced his theological statements and his craving for attention. Following an invitation from the English Defence League, Jones considered attending a rally in Luton, UK, in February 2011, prompting Hope not Hate to petition the Home Secretary to ban him. On January 2011, Home Secretary Theresa May announced Jones would be refused entry to the UK for the public good. A religious group placed a $1.2 million bounty on Jones' head, and Hezbollah announced a $2 million bounty. On April 22, 2011, Jones planned to visit the Islamic Center of America in Dearborn, Michigan, to protest sharia, but was arrested, tried, and jailed. Local authorities required him to post a $45,000 peace bond or go to trial; Jones contested the requirement, and the jury voted for a $1 peace bond, but Jones and co-pastor Wayne Sapp refused to pay. They were briefly jailed on First Amendment grounds and released the same night. On November 11, 2011, Wayne County Circuit Court Judge Robert Ziolkowski vacated the breach of peace ruling, citing denial of due process, and both men's criminal records were expunged. On April 22, 2012, shortly after being interviewed at WJBK, Jones' gun fired accidentally as he got into his car. On April 29, 2011, the city allowed Jones to protest in a designated "free speech zone" outside Dearborn City Hall, where Muslim protesters lined Michigan Avenue. About an hour into the protest, the crowd broke barricades and rushed the street, throwing water bottles and shoes at Jones' supporters, leading to at least one arrest. In 2010, Jones announced the Quran burning, which drew condemnation from a wide range of politicians and religious groups. Jones claimed he canceled the event and intended to meet with Feisal Abdul Rauf, the imam behind the Park51 mosque project, and later said he would never burn scriptures, though on March 20, 2011, he oversaw the burning. This prompted protests, including an attack in Afghanistan that resulted in at least 14 deaths. In April 2011, Jones said he was considering a trial of Muhammad for "crimes against humanity." The Dove World Outreach Center, a small congregation in Gainesville, first gained media attention in the late 2000s for its anti-Islamic and anti-homosexual messages. In 2009, the church posted a sign reading "Islam Is of the Devil" and several members sent their children to school wearing t-shirts with that message. The proposal began with Twitter messages on July 12 and a discussion on the now-removed Facebook group "Islam Is of the Devil," named after Jones' book. Jones invited Christians to burn the Quran to remember the 9/11 victims, to be held from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. The idea initially faced little support and opposition, but Religion News Service reported Jones claimed to have received Qurans to burn. CAIR refused to respond, while other religious groups did. On July 25, Jones posted a YouTube video holding up a Quran and saying it was responsible for 9/11 and looked like "the religion of the devil," which garnered significant media attention. On August 3, Gainesville Mayor Craig Lowe asked the world's media to ignore Jones' church as a "tiny fringe group and an embarrassment to our community," though coverage continued. Sunni scholars at al-Azhar University in Cairo issued a statement warning of "dangerous consequences" if Qurans were burned. U.S. President Obama condemned the plan, saying it would endanger U.S. troops abroad. American Muslims responded by celebrating September 11 as "Love Jesus Day," emphasizing Jesus as a messenger of God in Islam, and other groups promoted "Read the Quran Day" for international understanding. A Gainesville Interfaith Forum, established in November 2009, requested September 11 be declared "Interfaith Solidarity Day," a request honored by Mayor Lowe. The Forum scheduled a "Gathering for Peace, Understanding and Hope" on the day before the planned burning. Mayor Lowe referred to Dove World as a "tiny fringe group and an embarrassment to our community." Twenty local religious leaders gathered on September 2, 2010, to call for citizens to rally around Muslims. The National Association of Evangelicals recommended cancellation, the Southern Baptist Convention spoke out, and the World Evangelical Alliance stated the plans did not represent most Christians and dishonored the 9/11 victims. John Rankin of the Theological Education Institute launched a "Yes to the Bible, No to the Burning of the Quran" effort, and Jennifer Bryson advocated Christian intra-faith dialogue and rejection of "Burn a Quran Day." Feisal Abdul Rauf stated that the burning would have created a disaster in the Muslim world, strengthened radicals, and increased the risk of terrorist acts against America. He also said retracting the mosque plan would send a wrong message that "Islam is under attack in America." A group of American veterans of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars wrote an open letter to HuffPost urging the public to respect the values they risked their lives to protect, stating that hateful rhetoric toward Muslims exposes soldiers overseas. U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said it was regrettable that a pastor with a church of no more than fifty people could make such a plan and gain global attention, emphasizing it did not represent America or its leadership, and expressing hope the church would cancel. U.S. Secretary of Defense Robert Gates contacted Jones to ask him not to proceed. The U.S. embassy in Kabul issued a statement condemning the plans. Robert Gibbs, White House Press Secretary, criticized the plans, stating any activity putting troops in harm's way would be a concern. General David Petraeus said such actions mirror Taliban tactics and could cause significant problems, noting hundreds of Afghans protested in Kabul chanting "death to America" and throwing rocks at a military convoy. Military officials feared protests would spread, and the Pentagon hoped the intervention would convince Jones to cancel. Jones responded, saying he understood Petraeus' concerns and that they were legitimate, but insisted they must send a message to radical Islam that they would no longer be controlled by fear. Republicans in Congress criticized Jones, with House Minority Leader John Boehner stating that having a right to do something does not mean it is the right thing to do. Former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin called the plans "insensitive and an unnecessary provocation," and Republican 2008 presidential nominee John McCain and Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell argued the actions put American troops at risk. President Barack Obama stated on ABC News that Jones' plan was contrary to American values and would endanger American soldiers. One book distribution website, SacredBookSource.com, offered 1,001 free Qurans and 1,000 free Bibles for every Quran Jones destroyed. The German Evangelical Alliance formally dissociated itself from the Quran burning due to reports of Jones' past association with the alliance. The Al-Falluja web forum threatened a bloody war against America. Various Muslims, including Ahmadiyya, argued the Dove World Outreach Center does not follow true Christian teachings of tolerance and love, quoting Jesus: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you" (Matthew 5:44–45). Mirza Masroor Ahmad, Head of the Community, stated religious extremism, whether Christian or Muslim, is never a true reflection of religion. On August 27, about 100 people protested in Indonesia outside the U.S. Embassy. Roni Ruslan of Hizb ut-Tahrir said no one could control the reaction and urged the U.S. government and Christian leaders to stop the plan, calling it an insult to Islam and 1.5 billion Muslims. On September 4, thousands of Indonesians, mostly Muslims, participated in events organized by Hizbut Tahrir, with Rokhmat Labib calling the burning a provocation and predicting Muslims would fight back. The World Evangelical Alliance condemned the Quran burning plans. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints issued a statement saying a key tenet of their faith is freedom of worship and that burning any scriptural text is not a legitimate form of protest. Humanists International also criticized the plans. On Friday, September 10 in Fayzabad, thousands protested after Eid ul-Fitr prayers, throwing stones at a German-controlled NATO base. Initial reports said troops opened fire, killing up to three and injuring others, but a local police official said only local police were involved. Protesters broke down the first perimeter gate, beat Afghan security guards and police with sticks, and fired warning shots were allegedly fired upon. A local police chief estimated around 1,500 protesters, with 150 involved in the shooting incident. Private security guards fired at those trying to enter. NATO launched an investigation. General Zahir Khan of the Kabul police described the Quran burning as a thinly disguised pretext for anti-government rallies with Taliban attendance. Protests occurred in several Afghan provinces: Nimruz, Kunar, Nangarhar, Parwan, Baghlan, Kunduz, Balkh, and Farah. President Hamid Karzai condemned the burning, stating it could not harm the Quran, which is in the hearts and minds of one-and-a-half billion people, and that insulting the Quran is an insult to nations. Protests continued through the next two days, with three wounded on September 11 and four on September 12 as security forces shot at demonstrators, some armed with sticks or throwing stones, resulting in two deaths from severe gunshot wounds. On September 11, protests continued in Logar Province when security forces fired at demonstrators trying to storm government buildings, wounding four; stones were also thrown at the department for women's affairs. In Badakhshan, about a thousand protested in three districts, though police said it was peaceful. The prominent Qatar-based scholar Yusuf al-Qaradawi, despite condemning the desecration, stated responding to an assault with another assault is not acceptable.

doc_name: Dove World Outreach Center Quran-burning controversy
text: Protests erupted globally in response to the planned burning of Qurans, with demonstrations occurring in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Indonesia, Gaza, India, Kashmir, Somalia, Iran, Iraq, South Africa, Canada, Cuba, France, Germany, the United States, the Vatican City, NATO member countries, and the Organisation of the Islamic Conference. In Afghanistan, President Hamid Karzai condemned the act, stating that burning the Quran could not harm it as it resides in the hearts and minds of one-and-a-half billion people, and that insulting the Quran is an insult to nations. On September 11 and 12, Afghan security forces fired on protesters in Puli Alam, Logar Province, wounding four and resulting in two deaths from severe gunshot wounds; in Badakhshan, thousands protested peacefully in three districts. In Pakistan, small rallies with around 200 protesters took place in Karachi and Multan. In Indonesia, Gaza, and India, protests also occurred. On September 15, Randall Terry responded to reports of at least 20 deaths linked to the protests by comparing the situation to a woman being abused by a partner, arguing that she is not responsible for the violence. In Kashmir, protests escalated over several days, with demonstrators defying a military curfew on September 13, setting fire to a Christian missionary school and government buildings, resulting in at least 13 deaths, one policeman killed, and over 113 police and 45 protesters wounded; on September 12, a church was burned and a curfew was imposed in Punjab; in Poonch, three protesters were shot, and several government offices and vehicles were burned in clashes that left four protesters dead and 19 wounded; by September 16, the Hindustan Times reported a death toll of 90, attributing much of the unrest to the indefinite military curfew. In Somalia, Al-Shabaab organized a protest rally against the Quran-burning attended by thousands. Iran's Islamic Culture and Relations Organization labeled the Quran-burning proposal a "Zionist" insult; Iranian students protested outside the Swiss embassy, chanting slogans condemning the desecration on the anniversary of 9/11; the Iranian House of Cartoon hosted an online exhibition with over 30 cartoons from Iran, Turkey, Brazil, Ukraine, and other countries, condemning the desecration on themes of Devil against Holy Books and Terry Jones; Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki called the act "heinous" and accused Zionists of using it to provoke religious discord; Iran's ambassador to the UN, Mohammad Khazaee, filed a complaint to draw international attention and warn against the repercussions; parliament speaker Ali Larijani condemned the U.S. for its silence, urging Muslim nations to act, and warned American legislators of a "harsh fate" if they fail to respond; parliament member Mohammad Dehqan claimed Zionists use anti-Islamic sentiment to deflect attention from Palestine and to discourage conversions; head of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, Alaeddin Boroujerdi, said U.S. reluctance to react indicates approval of the act; Grand Ayatollahs Hossein Noori Hamedani and Naser Makarem Shirazi supported killing Quran-burners but required a religious judge's permission. In Iraq, Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani called the act "expression of hatred of Islam." A hacker named "Iraq Resistance" posted a voice-altered video under the byname "iqziad" claiming to have released the "Here you have" computer worm to demand respect for Islam, blaming Terry Jones, and stating he could "smash all of those infected, but I wouldn't"; the worm, discovered on August 20, targeted organizations including NASA, Walt Disney, and the Florida Department of Transportation, and produced spam that reached 10% of all email traffic on September 9. In South Africa, Johannesburg businessman Mohammed Vawda announced plans to burn the Bible on September 11 in response to the Quran-burning announcement; the Islamic lawyers' association, Scholars of the Truth, filed an injunction against him, which Judge Sita Kolbe of the Gauteng Division granted, prohibiting the burning; lawyer Yasmin Omar stated that freedom of expression is not unlimited if it harms others. Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper condemned the Quran-burning as "unqualified," saying "My God and my Christ is a tolerant God, and that's what we want to see in this world." Cuban former president Fidel Castro called the event a "huge media show" and questioned what FBI agents said to persuade Terry Jones to cancel. French Defence Minister Hervé Morin stated that the threatened Quran-burning and the subsequent ban on face coverings did not increase risks to French or NATO troops. German Chancellor Angela Merkel called the Florida event "plainly disrespectful – even abhorrent. It's simply wrong." Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono warned that the Quran-burning plans threatened world peace. Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei held the U.S. government and its politicians accountable, demanding punishment for the perpetrators; President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad called it a "Zionist plot against the teachings of all divine prophets." Lebanese President Michel Suleiman denounced the plan, stating it contradicts the teachings of Christianity, Islam, and Judaism and undermines interfaith dialogue. Pakistan's government strongly condemned the plan, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Abdul Basit stating it was against the spirit of any religion and outraged the Pakistani people, including Christians. In Gaza, Hamas Prime Minister Ismail Haniyeh called Terry Jones a "crazy priest who reflects a crazy Western attitude toward Islam and the Muslim nation." U.S. President Barack Obama warned that the stunt could endanger U.S. troops in Iraq and Afghanistan, called it an al-Qaeda recruitment tool, and urged cancellation, noting that U.S. law prevented action beyond local ordinances. The Vatican's Dicastery for Interreligious Dialogue issued a statement calling the burning an "outrageous and grave gesture." NATO Secretary General Anders Fogh Rasmussen said the church's plans violated NATO values and could negatively impact soldier security. The Organisation of the Islamic Conference expressed deep concern and alarm. United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said he was "deeply disturbed," adding that such a gesture would be intolerable by any religion. Some media attributed the event to sensationalism and "silly season." James Poniewozik of Time noted that fringe groups often receive coverage due to their strangeness and the timing coinciding with concerns over "Islamophobia" and the "Ground Zero mosque"; he argued that the story, by becoming news, now constitutes legitimate news. Slate's columnist Roger Simon responded to David Petraeus' remarks by stating the issue is not the images but the acts. Both the Associated Press and Fox News stated their intention to ignore the event. The conservative Powerline blog opposed the Quran-burning but attributed the dilemma to radical Muslim fanaticism, arguing that such behavior benefits those who burn Qurans by promoting the de facto outlawing of criticism of Islam. Michelle Malkin echoed Christopher Hitchens, lamenting "the eternal flame of Muslim outrage," claiming that even mundane items serve as tinder for jihadist retaliation. A Facebook page supporting the pastor's plan gained over 16,000 fans by the eve of the event, while opposition fans numbered in the hundreds of thousands. The Gainesville fire department refused to issue a burning permit; despite this, the church planned to proceed with the event, facing a potential fine. Following the July 2010 announcement, a bank holding a $140,000 mortgage on the church property demanded immediate repayment and canceled the insurance. A lighted sign and an acrylic cross were damaged by rocks. On September 8, 2010, Rackspace disconnected the Dove World Outreach website, citing a violation of its terms of use, not a constitutional issue. The city of Gainesville threatened to charge the church $200,000 for security costs, with the Alachua County Sheriff's Office estimating $100,000 spent on security, assigning 160 of 242 deputies to related duties on September 11. Terry Jones said he hoped the event would not lead to violence and reported receiving regular death threats; Evan Kohlmann of Flashpoint Global Partners noted that a suicide bomber threatened to drive a truck into the church and others discussed setting it on fire, though the seriousness was unclear. When death threats were mailed to The Gainesville Sun from Johnstown, Pa., the American Muslim Association of North America issued a statement signed by 15 imams, including Ahmed Al Mehdawi of the Islamic Center of Gainesville, condemning the threats. During Jones' September 11 visit to New York, Police Commissioner Ray Kelly said police would keep a close watch on him for safety. In March 2013, al-Qaeda's English-language magazine Inspire published a poster titled "Wanted dead or alive for crimes against Islam" featuring Terry Jones. Within hours of Jones' cancellation on September 9, Westboro Baptist Church member Megan Roper announced via Twitter that her church would proceed with a Quran-burning ceremony; her mother claimed the media had not covered the 2008 WBC Quran-burning as thoroughly as in 2010; Phelps announced his intention to burn the Quran and the American flag on September 11, which he did without incident. Duncan Philp of the Wyoming Tyranny Response Team obtained a permit to protest outside the Wyoming State Capitol from 11:00 to 13:00 on September 11, intending to set a Quran on fire or tear it up and dispose of the pieces in a garbage can to be burned privately; members of the local Unitarian Universalist Church planned a counter-protest, later describing the action as a test of free speech and stating they would take no action on state property. In Pueblo West, Colorado, a Quran was bolted to a stop sign during the weekend of September 11–12. In Nashville, Evangelical pastor Bob Old and another preacher burned a Quran with lighter fluid in a private yard; protesters came to his house but no confrontation occurred; he decided not to post the burning on YouTube. In lower Manhattan, protesters against the "Ground Zero mosque" took actions against the Quran.

doc_name: Dove World Outreach Center Quran-burning controversy
text: The Anny Response Team obtained a permit to protest outside the Wyoming State Capitol from 11:00 to 13:00 on September 11, expressing intent to set a Quran on fire at noon; if public burning was not allowed, they planned to tear up the Quran and move the pieces to a private business for burning. Members of the local Unitarian Universalist Church organized a counter-protest. The group later described the action as a test of free speech and stated they would not carry out any actions on state property. In Pueblo West, Colorado, a Quran was bolted to a stop sign during the weekend of September 11–12. In Nashville, Evangelical pastor Bob Old and another preacher burned a Quran with lighter fluid in a private yard; protesters visited his home but no confrontations occurred, and he decided not to post the burning on YouTube. In lower Manhattan, protesters against the "Ground Zero mosque" engaged in actions involving the Quran; one individual, later identified as a New Jersey transit worker, burned a few pages and was escorted away by police; he was subsequently fired for violating a code of conduct despite being off-duty, drawing criticism from New Jersey state senator Ray Lesniak and the American Civil Liberties Union, which argued that off-duty political expression should not lead to termination. In Texas, on the ninth anniversary of 9/11, a group of Christians, Muslims, Buddhists, and atheists gathered at Sam Houston Park to oppose evangelist David Grisham’s plan to burn the Quran; activist Isom removed the Quran from Grisham, who then left the park. Alex Stewart, a research lawyer in Brisbane, Australia, allegedly rolled "joints" using pages from the Quran and the Bible and smoked them in a YouTube video, which was quickly removed; many copies have since been shared, and Michael Cope of the Queensland Council for Civil Liberties stated it was not an offense under the Queensland Anti-Discrimination Act. Stewart was placed on leave by Queensland University of Technology’s vice-chancellor Peter Coaldrake pending a review under the university’s code of conduct, with Coaldrake stating the university was deeply disappointed and that such incidents cause community collateral damage; Stewart was returned to work on September 22 after offering an unreserved apology. A YouTube spokesperson noted they do not prescreen videos and typically respond to complaints by adding warnings about offensive content; HuffPost questioned why Quran-burning was treated as major news while many crimes, such as the prosecution of 12 U.S. soldiers for premeditated murder of Afghan civilians and keeping body parts as trophies, were not covered. Keith Richburg of The Washington Post in Beijing said professional journalists act as filters to prevent harmful information from spreading, warning that digital media undermines this gatekeeping role; American counterintelligence experts noted that without televised Quran burnings on the 9/11 anniversary, violent anti-American protests in Muslim countries would soon subside. A Quran was found shot and burned in the driveway of the Annoor Mosque in Knoxville, Tennessee; Knoxville police and the FBI began investigating it as a possible civil rights violation, threat, and hate crime. A YouTube video by user "MuslimKnoxvilleOrg" showing a Quran stuffed with bacon and doused with lighter fluid was also under investigation, though not immediately linked to the mosque. FBI Special Agent Richard L. Lambert stated that placing a burned Quran on mosque property could be interpreted as a threat of force, and federal charges were considered under a 1968 law prohibiting force to prevent religious practice, while state charges under Tennessee civil rights law and misdemeanor offenses like disorderly conduct were also explored. In Michigan, a burned Quran was found in front of the Islamic Center of East Lansing; local police and the FBI responded to the incident. Dawud Walid, director of Michigan’s Islamic council chapter, compared the act to painting a swastika on a synagogue or burning a cross on a black church. On September 21, the County Prosecutor ruled that the man who turned himself in would not face charges because the act was not a crime under Michigan’s criminal code. On the north side of Chicago, Illinois, a burned Quran and a letter were found on the sidewalk outside the Muslim Community Center over the September 11–12 weekend and were turned over to Chicago police’s bomb and arson unit. On September 9, Jones announced the cancellation of a planned Quran-burning event and a plan to fly to New York to meet with Imam Feisal Abdul Rauf; in an interview on September 11, he stated, "We will definitely not burn the Quran...Not today, not ever." Despite the cancellation, protesters from both sides attempted to reach the rally, but a heavy police presence was present; a visitor from Atlanta who tried to burn a Quran had his book and lighter seized by police. The World Evangelical Alliance contacted Jones, asking him to apologize, but he refused, saying, "We will not repent for standing up for the gospel," and claimed Christian churches had lost their courage to defend Christianity. As of October 22, 2010, Jones collected a new car offered as a reward by a New Jersey Hyundai dealership owned by former New York Giants player Brad Benson if he did not burn Qurans; Jones said he did not learn of the reward until several weeks after canceling the protest. On January 19, 2011, Jones was banned from entering the United Kingdom by British Home Secretary Theresa May after being invited to speak at a Right-Wing group, England is Ours, in Milton Keynes. On March 20, 2011, Dove World Outreach Center held a trial called "International Judge the Quran Day"; Jones played the role of a "judge" in traditional robes. The Quran was placed on trial for six hours, charged with responsibility for violence; the jury found it guilty of all charges and "sentenced" it to burning. Pastor Wayne Sapp then "executed" the Quran by burning it. In April 2011, Jones sought a permit to hold a rally at the Islamic Center of America in Dearborn, Michigan; a jury ruled that Jones and Sapp would breach the peace, and Judge Mark Somers set a bond of $1 for each, which they refused to pay; Somers remanded them to jail, and Jones was barred from the mosque area for three years. On November 11, 2011, Wayne County Circuit Court Judge Robert Ziolkowski vacated the breach of peace ruling against Jones and Sapp, citing denial of due process, and both men’s criminal records were expunged. After a sermon on April 1 in Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghanistan, angry demonstrators killed at least 12 people, including five Nepalese security guards and three UNAMA staff members; Jones denied responsibility. Pajhwok Afghan News reported the dead included Norwegian, Romanian, and Swedish nationals, two of whom were decapitated; BBC cited police general Abdul Rafu Taj, stating initial reports indicated they were shot in the head. Up to 2,000 protesters took to the streets in Kandahar on April 2, chanting anti-U.S. slogans, burning vehicles, hurling stones at police, torching a girls' high school, and burning a school bus; security forces killed nine protesters and injured 73; smaller protests occurred in other cities. The Gambian government called for the arrest of Terry Jones; Ebrima O. Camara, secretary general of civil service, described the burning as "heinous" and urged prosecution to proceed "as soon as possible." An affiliate website of Iran's Revolution Guard Cyber Defense Command quoted a report from Vatan-e Emrooz claiming Iranian border patrols were burning smuggled Bibles in Iran; on March 25, 2011, Iranian Ambassador to the UN Mohammad Khazaee condemned the burning and called for Jones’ prosecution. In southern Lebanon, students peacefully protested with Shia sheikh Hassan al-Zayyat outside the Lebanese International University to build the largest Quran on Earth, weighing 100 kg; Hezbollah has placed a $2.4 million bounty on pastor Terry Jones, according to the FBI. On March 22, 2011, Pakistanis protested in Punjab Christian neighborhoods and burned tires in front of a church; on the same day, Amir Hamza, leader of Pakistan’s banned Lashkar-e-Taiba, issued a $2.2 million fatwa for anyone who kills Terry Jones. On March 25, 2011, protests erupted in Pakistan, with Jamiat-e-Ulema-e-Islam organizing province-wide protests, including road blockages and burnings of effigies and American flags in Sindh. A man desecrated the Bible at the gates of Saint Anthony’s Catholic Church in Lahore to "avenge" Jones’ Quran burning; he was arrested by Pakistani police. The President of the Pakistani Bishops’ Conference, Lawrence Saldanha, called for Jones’ arrest, stating his Quran burning caused scandal and fury in the Muslim world and resulted in over 20 deaths; Saldanha urged the U.S. government to detain Jones. A South African Islamic organization, Scholars for Truth, turned to the country’s courts to prevent a fellow-Muslim from burning Bibles in retaliation to Jones’ threats. U.S. President Barack Obama strongly condemned the Quran burning, calling it an act of "extreme intolerance and bigotry" and the "outrageous" attacks by protesters, referring to them as "an affront to human decency and dignity," and stated, "No religion tolerates the slaughter and beheading of innocent people, and there is no justification for such a dishonorable and deplorable act." U.S. legislators, including Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, also condemned both the burning and the resulting violence. Gen. David Petraeus said, "This was a surprise," and "That action was hateful; it was intolerant." On April 4, 2011, two U.S. soldiers were shot and killed by an Afghan policeman, an attack attributed to anger over the Quran burning; the attacker was later killed in a shootout with NATO troops. The attacker was hailed as a hero and martyr by some in the local community, with his grave becoming an unofficial shrine and local mosques named after him; however, at least one local cleric stated the attack could not be justified on religious grounds.
